          Technical projects

          Projects in code, data and machine learning, mostly from my engineering degree.

          In progress · Deep learning coursework

          A convolutional neural network for handwritten digits

          A convolutional network with two convolution layers, trained on the MNIST handwriting dataset. I’ll analyse it through its loss curves, its accuracy on test data and how it converges.

          • CNNs
          • Deep learning
          • MNIST
          Algorithms · C++

          Finding a way out of a maze with A*, breadth-first and depth-first search

          Three classic search algorithms written in C++ to solve a maze. Depth-first search follows one path as far as it can, breadth-first search spreads out evenly and finds the shortest route, and A* uses an estimate of the distance to the exit to head straight for it.

          • A*
          • C++
          • Graph search
          • Pathfinding
          Coursework · C

          Handwritten digit recognition with neural networks built from scratch

          Neural networks written by hand, without machine learning libraries. I started with a perceptron telling a 0 from a 1, used the Widrow–Hoff rule to place the decision boundary evenly between the classes, and extended it to all ten digits. I then built a multi-layer perceptron (784 inputs, 100 hidden neurons, 10 outputs) trained with backpropagation on the MNIST handwriting dataset. I also measured how well the networks generalise by adding noise to the inputs.

          • Backpropagation
          • C
          • MNIST
          • Perceptrons
          Tool · Python

          Petri net simulator and analyser

          A graphical editor and analyser for coloured Petri nets, which model systems where many things happen at once. It explores every reachable state (depth-first and breadth-first), detects deadlocks, checks boundedness and analyses liveness using Tarjan’s algorithm.

          • Graph algorithms
          • Python
          • Systems modelling
          In progress · C, deep learning coursework

          Teaching an agent to play Breakout with deep reinforcement learning

          A deep Q-network written from scratch in C, with no machine learning libraries. I’m building the game and the agent: a network with 8 inputs, two hidden layers of 64 neurons and 3 possible actions, plus a replay memory and a target network. The results will be a learning curve and a report.

          • C
          • Deep Q-learning
          • Reinforcement learning
          Data analysis · R

          What makes a wine score well?

          Data analysis and data mining on how a wine’s chemical properties relate to its quality rating. I explored the data with tidyverse and ggplot2, then compared random forests, decision trees and neural networks for predicting quality.

          • ggplot2
          • Machine learning
          • R
          • tidyverse

          About

          I'm a French and British student in an integrated dual Master's: a Diplôme d'Ingénieur in Computer Engineering at CY Tech and a Master of Design in Global Design at CY École de Design, graduating in 2028. I work in English, French and Spanish.

          My way into AI safety and the societal impacts of technology is education: making information accessible and readable, so more people can discuss and think about these questions.

          Outside work, I repair phones and computers, draw and paint, take line dancing classes and play the guitar (badly). I also hold a brown belt in karate.

          Research interests

          The question running through my work: how do AI systems change the way people reason, discuss and decide, and can people still keep them in check?

          • Causal and evidential reasoningWhy people hold the beliefs they do: how they weigh evidence, judge causes and deal with disinformation, and what part technology plays in that.
          • Debate and collective reasoningHow opinions form in discussion, and what role debate plays in learning and in changing one's mind. Researchers call this argumentation, or collective reasoning.
          • Human oversight of AIHow well people can judge, evaluate and correct what an AI produces, and when they simply defer to it: the human side of scalable oversight and alignment. This is where I'm heading next.
          • Human–AI interactionHow an AI's behaviour shapes the way people think, speak and decide.AI peer study →

          Beyond my research, I care about access to information, child safety, education, the right to privacy and women's rights. I try to put these into practice in my projects by sharing what I learn openly and by organising events and discussions that bring people together.

          Publications

          1. First author: research article on how an AI peer's stance shapes collaborative discussion and decision-making. Under anonymous peer review, 2026. Results to follow after the decision.
          2. Co-author, poster: “Linking the IPBES Nature Futures Framework with the Transformative Change and the Nexus assessments”. World Biodiversity Forum, Davos, 2026. doi:10.5194/wbf2026-794

          How I work

          My research goes round the same loop. Take debate as a route to scalable oversight: can a person tell which of two AIs arguing with each other is right? At every stage, my value is as a translator between people who rarely speak the same language: engineers and designers, researchers and policymakers, experts and the public. I turn a technical question into a study people can take part in, and the results into something each audience can act on.
